Homonyms are made up of homophones and homographs.

A homophone is a word that has the same sound as another word but has a different meaning and may have a different spelling.

For example:
right and write
right (noun) and right (adjective)

A homograph is a word that has the same spelling as another word but has a different sound and a different meaning.

For example:
present (noun) and present (verb)
wind (noun) and wind (verb)
You stress you and I to add meaning and emphasis to a statement.

When you stress a word, you make it longer, louder and a little higher tone. You can put stress on a word to emphasize it and make your meaning clearer.
You stress you or I when you want to emphasize something about a person that is not expected.

For example:
I'm good. But how about you?

When you put stress on you, you shift the emphasis to the other person.
Read these sentences with stress on the bolded words:
I thought it went well but apparently she didn't.
You're the best writer on their team there!
You're not the problem there, she is!
If I were you, I'd write to someone in human resources.
And then there was that time when she was hungover and you had to present the birthday present.
when someone works with only one other person
Example: How did the one-on-one with your boss go?
These are words you use to talk about reactions and behavior in different situations.
to tell (someone) about possible danger or trouble
Example: I had to warn her that that was against the dress code.
something that appears to be true based on what is known
Example: I thought it went well but apparently she didn't.
a piece of information that someone forgets
Example: She's always so stressed. Maybe it slipped her mind.
a sick feeling or condition that comes after drinking too much alcohol
Example: Do you remember the time when she was hungover at work?
a person who is a negative influence
Example: She sounds like a real piece of work!
With a partner, write down as many homonyms as you can think of.
On your own, write a story or dialogue and try to include as many homonym pairs from your list as you can.
When you are finished, share your writing with your partner. Who used the most homonyms correctly?

images.text:
Vanessa: Hello?
Sally: Hi Vanessa! How are you?
Vanessa: I'm good. But what about you? How did the one-on-one with your boss go? You met with her, didn't you?
Sally: Yes, and I thought that it went well but apparently she didn't. She told another woman at work that I'm being difficult and I'm not a team player.
Vanessa: You're not a team player? You're the best writer on their team there! And you always help everyone else, don't you? If I were you, I'd write to someone in human resources about her, right away! You're not the problem here, she is!

Sally: I'm really confused by her behavior. I've tried to be helpful to her from the start. Remember when she had worn jeans to work a couple times and I had to warn her that that was against the dress code? And that time when she asked me to sell her cell phone?
Vanessa: And then there was that time when she was hungover and you had to present the birthday present to the president of the company! She remembers these things, doesn't she?

Sally: She's always so stressed. Maybe it slipped her mind.
Vanessa: That's no excuse! You're not going to excuse her, are you? She sounds like a real piece of work!
Sally: By the way, she asked me to buy her a pair of pears for her lunch.
Vanessa: You really do need to get away, don't you? I'll take you to a tropical isle for a holiday.
